ABSTRACT Visual object tracking is a challenging computer vision task that aims to localize a target
throughout a video given its initial state. Although recent trackers have significantly advanced visual object
tracking, many do not explicitly incorporate image-quality degradations in their training objective functions
or architectures, leaving target localization vulnerable to motion blur, resolution loss, sensor noise, and
compression artifacts that weaken fine details and boundary cues. In this paper, we propose an efficient
Siamese-style tracker called, InvTrack, that learns degradation-invariant representations for robust target
matching. InvTrack is formulated as a tracking-specific integration of degradation-invariant learning within
an efficient single-object Siamese framework, where clean–degraded consistency is enforced on both the
template and search branches, the resulting clean and degraded matching cues are fused before the final
target-state prediction, and low-pass residual modules are used for more stable feature extraction. During
training, paired clean and degraded template and search samples act as structured augmentation, while
invariant losses regularize the network to learn more degradation-robust representations. This design im-
proves the generalization capability of the tracker and leads to more reliable performance under challenging
imaging conditions. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate that InvTrack achieves
state-of-the-art results on five datasets, namely TrackingNet with 85.2 AUC, 89.3 PNorm, and 84.2 P;
AVisT with 55.3 AO, 63.7 OP50, and 46.0 OP75; UAV123 with 71.9 AUC; OTB100 with 71.5 AUC; and
NfS30 with 69.1 AUC, while also obtaining highly competitive performance on GOT-10k with 75.7 AO,
84.6 SR0.5, and 73.1 SR0.75, and LaSOT with 72.1 AUC, 81.6 PNorm, and 78.5 P. These results confirm
that the proposed tracking-specific integration of degradation-invariant learning yields strong robustness
and generalization across diverse tracking benchmarks.
INDEX TERMS Visual object tracking, single-object tracking, invariant feature learning, image-quality
degradation, Siamese tracking.
I. INTRODUCTION
Robust visual object tracking is one of the most sig-
nificant tasks in computer vision, with applications in
video monitoring analysis [1], self-driving cars [2], [3],
visual surveillance [4], human–machine interaction [5], au-
tonomous robots [6], aerial-view tracking [7], augmented
reality [8], sports analysis [9], surgery [10], and ocean
exploration [11], to name a few. The task of visual object
tracking aims to estimate the target object’s location in every
frame of a video, given only its initial state in the first
frame. Despite significant progress in recent years, tracking
remains highly challenging due to appearance variations
caused by occlusion, low-resolution cameras, deformation,
out-of-view motion, motion blur, fast motion, illumination
variation, scale variation, and background clutter [12]. To

range of approaches over the years.
Existing visual object tracking methods can be broadly
categorized into four families: generative, discriminative,
collaborative, and deep learning–based trackers. Generative
methods [14], [15], [16], [17] attempt to match candidate
regions with the target appearance model, selecting the
most similar region as the predicted location. Discrimi-
native methods [18], [19], [20], [21] instead treat track-
ing as a binary classification problem, learning a deci-
sion boundary to separate the target from the background.
Collaborative approaches [22], [23] combine generative
and discriminative components to exploit their comple-
mentary strengths. Traditional approaches generally rely
on handcrafted features, making them fragile in com-
plex conditions. In contrast, deep learning–based track-
ers [24], [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30], [31] leverage
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers to
extract more robust representations in an end-to-end manner,
leading to significant performance improvements.
Recent state-of-the-art trackers have increasingly adopted
deep neural networks, particularly convolutional networks
and transformers, to achieve superior performance. Siamese-
based trackers [71], [72], [73] pioneered the use of similarity
learning for robust matching between the template and
search regions, relying on convolutional backbones such as
ResNet [40] to generate comparable embeddings. Anchor-
free approaches such as Ocean [63] and Alpha-Refine [67]
continued to employ CNN feature extractors (e.g., ResNet-
50) while improving localization accuracy through anchor-
free classification and regression heads. With the advent of
transformers, hybrid trackers like TransT [75], STARK [74],
and MixFormer [60] combined CNN-based feature extractors
with transformer modules, where local CNN features were
enriched by the global dependencies captured through self-
attention. More recent advances such as OSTrack [46],
AiATrack [66], and SeqTrack [46] moved away from CNNs
entirely, adopting pure Vision Transformer (ViT) [90] back-
bones (e.g., ViT-B/16, ViT-S/16) to directly model long-
range contextual representations from image patches.
Despite these impressive achievements, the generalizabil-
ity of current deep neural network–based trackers remains
less than satisfactory. In real-world scenarios, video frames
are often affected not only by degradations such as motion
blurring, but also by occlusions and illumination changes.
These factors significantly reduce the robustness of feature
extractors that assume clean, high-quality inputs, thereby
limiting the reliability of existing methods in practical ap-
plications.
In realistic scenarios, video frames often suffer from im-
age-quality degradations that make visual tracking signifi-
cantly more challenging. Examples include motion blur, res-
olution loss, sensor noise, and compression artifacts, all of
which can weaken target representations and degrade match-
ing reliability. Despite the importance of this point, compar-
atively less attention has been paid to designing learning
algorithms for visual object tracking networks that explicitly
improve robustness against such input-quality degradations
in real-world setups.
In recent deep tracking frameworks, the general formu-
lation aims to extract meaningful representations from a
given template frame and the current video frame, and
then compute their spatial similarity to localize the target.
These frameworks commonly employ a backbone network
(e.g., ResNet-50, ViT-S/16) to extract deep features, followed
by a cross-attention or correlation module to compare the
embeddings. The outputs are then passed to separate classi-
fication and regression heads for target presence estimation
and bounding box prediction. Such models are trained end-
to-end on large-scale video datasets, optimizing for stan-
dard tracking losses. This paradigm has yielded significant
improvements across several benchmarks, especially under
controlled or moderately challenging conditions.
However, these trackers often assume ideal input con-
ditions, where both template and search regions are clear
and well-illuminated. To improve resilience, some methods
attempt to introduce architectural enhancements, such as
context-aware attention, refinement stages, or temporal mem-
ory modules. For instance, approaches like KeepTrack [29]
and AutoMatch [68] enhance the matching process using
temporal cues, while Alpha-Refine [67] incorporates iterative
refinements to correct localization errors. Nevertheless, most
of these solutions operate at the architectural level and still
rely on features extracted from potentially degraded frames.
In other words, although state-of-the-art trackers have be-
come deeper and more accurate, they largely overlook the
explicit modeling of input imperfections—such as blur, low
resolution, or occlusions—which are inevitable in real-world
environments.
Based on the above discussion, three main research gaps
can be identified in current visual object tracking literature.
First, although recent trackers have become increasingly
powerful in terms of backbone design and matching strategy,
most of them are still trained under the implicit assumption
of clean input observations and do not explicitly enforce
robustness against input-quality degradations. Second, the
majority of existing approaches improve performance mainly
through architectural refinement, while comparatively less
attention has been paid to learning objectives that directly
regularize the extracted representations to remain stable un-
der degraded imaging conditions. Third, degradation-aware
designs explored in related settings are often tailored to spe-
cific scenarios, such as low-light multi-object tracking [51],
and are not directly formulated for efficient single-object
Siamese template–search matching. These gaps motivate
the development of a tracking-specific degradation-invariant
learning framework that can improve robustness under real-
istic image-quality degradations while preserving efficiency.
It is seen from the above paragraphs that much of the
recent effort in the community has focused on designing

can remain limited in realistic scenarios. Therefore, in addi-

that remain stable under degradations such as blur, resolution

Motivated by the above discussion, in this paper we pro-
pose InvTrack, a deep learning–based visual object tracking
framework designed to learn more robust feature representa-
tions and, consequently, improve tracking performance under
challenging imaging conditions. In practical scenarios, video
frames are frequently affected by image-quality degradations
such as motion blur, resolution loss, sensor noise, and com-
pression artifacts, which can weaken target representations
and degrade matching reliability. Therefore, beyond design-
ing stronger backbones and prediction heads, it is important
to explicitly guide the tracker toward degradation-robust fea-
ture extraction.
To realize this objective, our proposed InvTrack scheme
has three main novelties. First, InvTrack introduces a degra-
dation-invariant learning formulation for Siamese single-ob-
ject tracking, where clean–degraded feature consistency is
enforced on both the template and search branches. Second,
it introduces a degradation-aware template–search matching
mechanism in which clean and degraded matching cues are
fused before the carrying out the tasks of classification and
bounding-box regression. Third, it proposes a residual dense
block built from low-pass residual modules each combin-
ing SConv, a standard convolutional path, and residual fea-
ture propagation, to suppress unstable high-frequency arti-
facts while preserving discriminative structural cues. In our
framework, SConv is embedded inside the proposed low-pass
residual modules of a Siamese tracking backbone, feature
alignment is performed between clean and synthetically de-
graded template/search features, and TV-based regularization
is used to stabilize the clean–degraded feature discrepan-
cies. These components are then coupled with response-map
fusion to produce more reliable degradation-aware match-
ing cues before target-state prediction. This differentiates the
proposed method from degradation-aware design developed
for other setting, particularly the low-light multi-object track-
ing framework of Wang et al.
[51]. In that work, SConv
is used inside an adaptive low-pass downsampling module,
while feature alignment and TV-based regularization are ap-
plied to features extracted from paired well-lit and low-light
images in a tracking-by-detection pipeline.
In this context, the main contribution of InvTrack lies
in a tracking-specific formulation of degradation-invariant
learning for single-object tracking. Specifically, InvTrack
introduces three main components: clean–degraded consis-
tency imposed symmetrically on both the template and
search branches across multiple backbone stages; degrada-
tion-aware template–search matching, where the resulting
clean/degraded response maps are fused before classification
and bounding-box regression; and a proposed residual dense
block built from low-pass residual modules that combine
SConv, a standard convolutional path, and residual feature
propagation to suppress unstable high-frequency artifacts
while preserving discriminative structural cues. The frame-
work is trained on standard single-object tracking datasets
with on-the-fly synthetic degradations, including motion blur,
resolution loss, sensor noise, and compression artifacts. This
differentiates the proposed method from degradation-aware
designs developed for other settings, such as low-light multi-
object tracking
[51], and clarifies the role of InvTrack
as a tracking-specific integration tailored to robust target
matching under degraded imaging conditions.
In this paper, the term invariant feature learning specif-
ically refers to robustness against input-quality degrada-
tions. To this end, the proposed tracking pipeline enforces
the feature extraction process of both template and search
frames to remain consistent under clean and degraded in-
puts. Concretely, the network is trained so that the features
extracted from clean template/search inputs and from their
synthetically degraded counterparts remain aligned. There-
fore, the targeted invariance concerns degradations such as
blur, downsampling, additive noise, and JPEG compression,
rather than a generic invariance to all nuisance factors.
As a result, the tracker learns feature maps that are more
stable under these degradations, which in turn benefits both
target classification and bounding-box regression, leading to
improved tracking accuracy and robustness.
In addition to the invariant feature learning strategy,
the backbone is enhanced with a low-pass residual mod-
ule (LPRM) embedded within residual dense blocks. Each
LPRM incorporates spatial low-pass convolution (SConv)
[51], where the convolution kernel is constrained through
softmax normalization to promote low-pass behavior. This
operation suppresses unstable high-frequency noise while
preserving structural information, allowing the network to
produce denoised yet discriminative features that remain
more consistent across varying input qualities.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec-
tion II, we review related work on object tracking and
invariant feature learning. In Section III, we present the
proposed framework, including the invariant feature learn-
ing mechanism, image-quality degradation processes, and
the classification/regression heads. Extensive experimental
settings and results on seven benchmarks are reported in
Section IV. Finally, concluding remarks and future directions
are provided in Section V.
II. Related Work
In this section, we review prior works pertinent to our visual
object tracking framework.
A. Visual Object Tracking
With the rise of deep learning, modern trackers increasingly
leverage CNNs and transformers to boost accuracy and
robustness. ECO [24] revisited the discriminative correlation
filter formulation with (i) a factorized convolution operator
that reduces parameters, (ii) a compact generative model
of the training sample distribution that cuts memory and
computation, and (iii) an improved update strategy that
enhances robustness. Building on this direction, ATOM [25]
introduced a dual-branch design with an IoU-based target es-
timation module (learned offline) and an online classification
branch to distinguish the target from distractors. DiMP [26]
further unified these ideas into an end-to-end framework that
learns a powerful discriminative model by exploiting both
target and background cues, iteratively refining the tracker
to improve separation and reduce prediction error.

Together, these advances illustrate a progression from
efficient correlation filters to discriminative modeling and

Siamese-based trackers have become a dominant paradigm
in visual tracking by modeling object similarity via metric
learning. The core idea is to embed the template and search
region into a shared feature space using weight-tied back-
bones and to localize via cross-correlation. The pioneering
SiamFC [72] framed tracking as similarity learning and
achieved real-time performance with a lightweight fully
convolutional design. Subsequent works strengthened local-
ization and representation: SiamRPN introduced region pro-
posals within the Siamese pipeline [73], while SiamRPN++
leveraged deeper backbones (e.g., ResNet-50), layer-wise
feature aggregation, and efficient depth-wise operations to
improve accuracy and runtime [73]. Extensions incorpo-
rated richer outputs and attention: SiamMask added instance
segmentation for tighter localization under clutter and oc-
clusion [71]; SiamAttn employed deformable attention and
region refinement to enhance discriminative features [71];
SiamDW explored deeper/wider networks (e.g., ResNet-101)
for stronger feature expressivity [73]; and SiamR-CNN fused
Siamese matching with R-CNN style proposal refinement to
better handle fast motion and complex backgrounds [73].
More recently, anchor-free formulations such as SiamBAN
and SiamCAR reduced reliance on anchors and directly
regressed boxes from similarity maps, improving adaptability
to target scale and aspect ratio [74], [75].
Beyond architectural advances, learning formulations have
broadened the Siamese paradigm. Unsupervised variants [56]
avoid manual annotations by exploiting contrastive objec-
tives and data augmentation to generate pseudo-labels, reduc-
ing annotation cost while preserving competitive accuracy.
Ranking-based training [61] optimizes a pairwise ranking
loss to sharpen target/non-target separation in cluttered
scenes. Automatch [68] adapts feature alignment on the fly
to cope with appearance variation, improving robustness to
scale changes and target deformation. Together, these lines of
work chart a progression from early cross-correlation base-
lines to proposal-enhanced, attention-augmented, anchor-
free, and adaptive-matching designs within the Siamese
family.
Transformers have recently gained traction in visual track-
ing for their ability to capture global spatial–temporal de-
pendencies via self-attention [39]. Early single-object ef-
forts replaced correlation-style matching with attention to
directly relate template and search features: TransT in-
troduced a transformer encoder–decoder for target–search
interaction [75], while STARK incorporated explicit tempo-
ral modeling to better handle appearance change and mo-
tion [74]. Hybrid designs coupled transformers with strong
discriminative heads—TrDiMP fused a transformer encoder
with the DiMP family [76], and ToMP refined model predic-
tion through target-aware attention [30]. Unified transformer
trackers integrated localization and classification within one
architecture [57]. Additional enhancements focused on con-
textual reasoning and robustness: KeepTrack modeled tar-
get–context associations [29]; SeqTrack cast tracking as

Although recent deep trackers have achieved strong perfor-
mance through improved backbones, attention mechanisms,
and refinement heads, most of them primarily focus on
enhancing template–search interaction under standard input
conditions. In contrast, the contribution of InvTrack lies
not in introducing an entirely new primitive module, but in
integrating degradation-invariant learning into a single-object
Siamese tracking framework. More specifically, InvTrack
differs from related deep tracking works in three aspects:
(i) it explicitly trains both the template and search branches
with paired clean/degraded inputs, rather than relying only
on stronger matching architectures; (ii) it enforces feature-
level consistency under degradations and combines this with
clean/degraded response-map fusion before prediction; and
(iii) it incorporates low-pass residual modules within the
backbone to improve robustness under degraded imaging
conditions while preserving efficiency. Therefore, the pro-
posed contribution is a tracking-specific degradation-robust
formulation rather than a claim of entirely new low-level
building blocks.
B. Invariant Feature Learning
Modern approaches prioritize invariant feature learning, aim-
ing for representations that remain stable under corrup-
tions, domain shifts, and sampling bias to deliver consistent
downstream performance. Concretely, FIFO learns visibility-
invariant features by aligning clear–foggy representations
so semantics persist under haze [80]; DALSCLIP induces
domain-invariant vision–language embeddings for CLIP by
aggregating heterogeneous sources [81]; the long-tailed clas-
sification work extracts class-sufficient yet distribution-stable
features to mitigate head-class bias [82]; DIFLF promotes
domain-invariant statistics for single-source generalization
in medical imaging [83]; and SIL provides a principled
formulation that retains label sufficiency while discarding
environment-specific variability, yielding shift-robust repre-
sentations [84]. Related efforts further encourage invariance
via adversarial representation learning that disentangles nui-
sance/private attributes while preserving task-relevant infor-
mation [92]; unsupervised domain adaptation with masked-
prediction objectives that drive domain-invariant feature
enhancement across conditions [93]; and source-data-free
cross-domain transfer that seeks domain-invariant features
without access to source data [94].

A related tracking effort is the work of Wang et al. [51],

is specialized for paired well-lit/low-light multi-object track-

pression artifacts.
III. Methodology
Let x[m, n, t] (0 ≤m ≤M −1, 0 ≤n ≤N −1, 0 ≤t ≤
T −1) denote a video sequence of spatial resolution M ×N
with T temporal frames. We refer to y[m, n] = x[m, n, 0] as
the template image and to z[m, n, t] = x[m, n, 1 : T −1] as
the subsequent video frames in which the target appearing
in y[m, n] must be tracked. For simplicity, we denote the
template image and search frames by y and z[t], respectively.
Our objective in this paper is to design an efficient object
tracking function f(·), which receives the template image y
and the search frame z[t], and outputs the predicted target-

As mentioned in Section I, the task of tracking remains
challenging because the object in different frames of z[t]
may appear at different scales and under degraded imag-
ing conditions. In the present work, we explicitly target
robustness to input-quality degradations such as motion blur,
resolution loss, additive noise, and compression artifacts.
These imperfections make detecting the object of interest in
z[t] extremely challenging, which in turn deteriorates both
classification and bounding-box regression performance. In
view of these explanations, it is crucial to design a robust
high-performance object tracking function f(·), which is able
to provide superior results by generating rich sets of feature
maps for a wide range of video frames with different object
appearances and properties.
In order to address the above-mentioned challenges for
training the object tracking function f(·), we aim at improv-
ing the feature generation capability of f(·) for various video
frames z[t]’s, and therefore, assure that it could produce rich
features that are useful for tracking different objects. For
achieving this superior feature generation capability, there
exist two general approaches, namely, improving feature
learning capability of f(·), and designing novel neural net-
work architectures for it.
We first focus on our idea for the initial approach, i.e.,
enhancing the feature learning capability of f(·). A suitable
function f(·) is able to detect the object of interest in z[t]
at any challenging scenario. The tracking function f(·) with
such a robust feature generation ability can be designed by
leveraging the concept of invariant feature learning.
In this work, the targeted invariance is explicitly defined as
robustness to input-quality degradations. Concretely, given
the clean template image y and the clean search frame
z[t], we generate their degraded counterparts yd = D(y)
and z[t]d = D(z[t]) through a synthetic degradation operator
D(·). The objective of the proposed invariant learning mod-
ule is then to enforce consistency between the feature repre-
sentations extracted from the clean inputs and those extracted
from their degraded counterparts. In this way, the learned
invariance is not generic, but specifically refers to robustness
against degradations such as blur, downsampling, additive
noise, and JPEG compression through clean/degraded feature
consistency.
The degradation-robustness mechanism of InvTrack is
achieved through three complementary ingredients. First, the
degradation operator D(·) generates paired clean/degraded
template–search inputs during training, which acts as a struc-
tured augmentation strategy. Second, the invariant learning
objective regularizes the tracker by enforcing consistency
between clean and degraded feature representations, while
the TV term promotes spatial stability. Third, the back-
bone is enhanced with low-pass residual modules based on
SConv, which suppress unstable high-frequency artifacts at
the architectural level. Therefore, the targeted invariance is
achieved through a combination of augmentation, loss-based
regularization, and architectural design.
These three components play distinct roles in the proposed
framework. The degradation pipeline is responsible only for
generating paired clean/degraded inputs and therefore de-
fines the training perturbation space. The invariant loss op-
erates at the representation level by reducing the discrep-
ancy between features extracted from the clean and degraded
branches, while the TV term further encourages spatial sta-
bility. In contrast, the low-pass residual modules act at the ar-
chitectural level by suppressing unstable high-frequency ar-
tifacts inside the backbone. Hence, the degradation operator,
the invariant objective, and the low-pass modules contribute
through input generation, loss regularization, and feature-
extraction design, respectively.
No additional invariant-feature components are used be-
yond these three elements.

Fig. 2 illustrates the architecture of the proposed residual

IV. Experiments
In this section, we first present the experimental setup
and implementation details used for training and evaluating
the proposed InvTrack. We then compare InvTrack with
state-of-the-art tracking methods on multiple benchmark
datasets and provide an attribute-level analysis on LaSOT
to further examine its behavior under challenging sequence
conditions. Next, we analyze the performance impact of the
main components of the proposed design through focused
ablation studies, followed by a hyper-parameter sensitivity
analysis of the loss-weight configuration. Finally, we report
the computational complexity and runtime performance of
the proposed tracker.
A. Experimental Setup and Implementation Details
For training the proposed InvTrack network, we utilize the
training splits of TrackingNet [37], LaSOT [36], GOT-
10k [35], and COCO [64], following the standard protocol
that excludes the 1,000 restricted sequences from the GOT-
10k training set. The image degradation process does not
rely on any auxiliary dataset; instead, these same training
samples are used to generate paired clean/degraded inputs
for degradation-invariant learning. For the video datasets,
namely TrackingNet, LaSOT, and GOT-10k, template–search
pairs are sampled from the same sequence following the
standard Siamese tracking protocol [72]. For COCO, which
is a still-image dataset, pseudo template–search pairs are
generated through spatial augmentation, following the com-
mon practice of constructing tracking pairs from image
datasets in Siamese-style trackers
[73]. For each sampled
template–search pair, the degradation operator D(·) is ap-
plied online to both the template and the search inputs to
generate their degraded counterparts. Therefore, the degraded
samples are created on-the-fly during training rather than
being precomputed or drawn from a separate degraded-data
corpus.
Unless otherwise stated, each training sample consists of a
template crop resized to 128×128 and a search crop resized
to 256×256, with an effective output stride of 16. During
inference, no synthetic degradation is applied; the tracker
operates on the original template crop and the current search
crop. The clean and degraded template–search feature inter-
actions are generated through four padded depthwise cross-
correlation response maps, which are concatenated and then
passed through the refinement function ϕ(·) before classifi-
cation and bounding-box regression. This inference descrip-
tion is consistent with the architecture summary reported in
Table 1.
For evaluation, we report Area Under the Curve (AUC),
Precision (P), Normalized Precision (PNorm), Average Over-
lap (AO), and Success Rate (SR), together with OP50 and
OP75 for AVisT. More specifically, TrackingNet and LaSOT
are evaluated using AUC, P, and PNorm; GOT-10k is evaluated
using AO together with SR at different overlap thresholds;
AVisT is evaluated using AO together with overlap preci-
sion at thresholds 0.50 and 0.75, denoted OP50 and OP75;
and UAV123, OTB100, and NfS30 are evaluated using AUC.
These metrics are computed on the predicted bounding boxes
across frames to assess both localization accuracy and overall
tracking robustness.
The proposed tracker is optimized by minimizing the
composite objective using the AdamW optimizer [41] with
a weight decay of 10−5. In the proposed InvTrack, the
components associated with degradation-invariant learning
consist of: (i) the image degradation operator used during
training to generate paired clean/degraded inputs, (ii) the
invariant objective composed of the feature-similarity and
TV regularization terms, and (iii) the low-pass residual
modules (LPRMs) embedded in the shared feature-extrac-
tion backbone. Among these components, only the LPRMs
correspond to additional trainable architectural layers; the
degradation operator is used only to generate training inputs,
and the invariant objective acts as a loss-based regular-
izer. The trainable backbone components associated with
this design, including the LPRMs, are optimized with a
learning rate of 5 × 10−5, while the classification and re-
gression heads use a learning rate of 5 × 10−4. Training
is carried out on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU
with a batch size of 64 for 250 epochs, where each
epoch contains 72,000 sampled pairs. The learning rate
is reduced by a factor of 10 after epoch 200 to ensure
stable convergence. Unless otherwise stated, all benchmark
results reported in this paper are obtained using this same
optimization setup together with the loss-weight configu-
ration (λcls, λreg, λSIM, λT V ) = (1.0, 1.2, 0.6, 0.1), which
was selected based on the hyper-parameter sensitivity anal-

C. Ablation Studies
To better understand the performance impact of the main
components of InvTrack, we conduct a focused component-
level ablation study. It is recalled that the main compo-
nents of the proposed scheme are: (i) the use of image-
quality degradations during the training process to generate
clean/degraded template–search pairs for the Siamese track-
ing network; (ii) the SConv-based low-pass residual module
design, which is used in the proposed backbone to suppress
high-frequency artifacts while preserving useful structural
information; (iii) the invariant feature learning loss function,
composed of the feature-similarity and TV regularization
components, which facilitates the feature representations
extracted from the original and degraded branches to be
consistent; and (iv) the response-map fusion strategy, which
fuses the four depthwise cross-correlation maps, namely
clean–clean, clean–degraded, degraded–clean, and degraded–
degraded matching cues, before classification and bounding-
box regression. In our ablation study, we isolate these
components, by removing, one at a time, the clean/degraded
training process, replacing the SConv-based low-pass resid-
ual module design with a standard convolutional, removing
invariant loss, and disabling the response-map fusion and
study the impact of each of these removals on the tracking
performance.

during training. Accordingly, only the original template
and search inputs, y and z[t], are processed by the
Siamese tracking network, while the degraded inputs

architecture itself is kept unchanged; however, since no
clean/degraded feature pairs are available, the invariant
objective LINV , including the feature-similarity and
TV regularization losses, is also removed. Thus, this
variant is trained only with Lcls and Lreg. In addition,
the matching stage is reduced from four clean/degraded
depthwise cross-correlations to a single clean–clean
depthwise cross-correlation between yo and zo
t, and no
response-map fusion is required. This variant evaluates

Overall, the ablation study shows that the main compo-
nents of InvTrack are complementary. The clean/degraded
training process exposes the tracker to perturbed template–

high-frequency artifacts, the feature-similarity and TV reg-
ularization losses reduce clean–degraded feature drift, and
the response-map fusion stage improves the use of multi-
ple template–search matching cues before prediction. When
combined, these components allow InvTrack to achieve the
best performance on both TrackingNet and LaSOT.

V. Conclusion
Visual object tracking in real-world scenarios remains chal-
lenging when the input frames are affected by image-qual-
ity degradations such as motion blur, resolution loss, ad-
ditive noise, and compression artifacts. To address this is-
sue, this paper presented InvTrack, a tracking-specific inte-
gration of degradation-invariant learning within an efficient
single-object tracking framework. The proposed method en-
forces clean–degraded feature consistency on both the tem-
plate and search branches and further improves robustness
through low-pass residual modules embedded in the back-
bone. By combining structured degradation-based augmenta-
tion, invariant loss regularization, and architectural enhance-
ment, InvTrack learns feature representations that are more
stable under degraded imaging conditions and beneficial for
both classification and bounding-box regression. Extensive
experiments on multiple tracking benchmarks demonstrate
that the proposed framework achieves strong and competitive
performance compared with recent state-of-the-art trackers,
while maintaining a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.
